claims.text: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys exhibit a mixture of FCC and BCC phases.
The baseline equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has a desirable balance of high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Al content modulates local lattice distortion in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys through atomic-size mismatch.
Increasing Al content increases atomic-size mismatch.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch raises lattice-distortion strain energy.
Lattice-distortion energy shifts the free-energy balance between FCC and BCC structures.
The Al-induced change in lattice distortion typically favors BCC stabilization over a mixed or competing phase structure.
Moderately increasing Al relative to the equiatomic baseline will measurably increase local lattice distortion.
Moderately increasing Al relative to the equiatomic baseline will increase the BCC phase fraction.
The Al-driven phase shift will correlate with changes in mechanical and environmental performance.
Lattice-distortion-mediated phase evolution supports retention of high-temperature strength.
Lattice-distortion-mediated phase evolution supports retention of corrosion resistance.
Lattice-distortion-mediated phase evolution supports retention of radiation tolerance.
Lattice-distortion-mediated phase evolution supports retention of cryogenic toughness.
An optimal balance of properties occurs before deleterious intermetallic precipitation begins.
XRD peak broadening or EXAFS can quantify the relevant local lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism applies only to small compositional deviations around the equiatomic composition.
At large Al deviations or after introducing other strongly size-mismatched elements, chemical ordering or other thermodynamic mechanisms may dominate phase stability.
The controlled comparison varies Al concentration while holding the ratios of Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni and the processing conditions constant.
